claims.source: Analyzing the tissue expression of E(z)-downregulated genes using Fly Atlas (Leader et al., 2018) showed that 49% are predominantly expressed in the testis or male accessory gland (Figure 3C), including most of the general gene expression isoforms discussed above.
claims.evidence: This is based on tissue expression analysis using Fly Atlas.

claims.claim: CG43088 is related to human harbinger-transpose-derived-1.
claims.source: CG43088 is related to human harbinger-transpose-derived-1 and shows promoter-associated peaks of ATAC and H3K27ac only in GSCs (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is based on sequence homology and chromatin data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: In E(z)[GLKD] early follicles CG43088 becomes threefold overexpressed relative to GSC levels and 400-fold overexpressed relative to early wild type follicles.
claims.source: In E(z)[GLKD] early follicles CG43088 become threefold overexpressed relative to GSC levels (127±10.2 vs 40±9.46 tpm) and 400-fold overexpressed relative to early wild type follicles (0.28±0.080 tpm).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data comparing E(z) knockdown to wild type.

claims.claim: escargot encodes a snail class transcription factor needed to maintain male (but not female) GSCs.
claims.source: escargot, encoding a snail class transcription factor needed to maintain male (but not female) GSCs, retains an open promoter in early follicles, but is downregulated (GSC: 91±0.11 tpm; OVS6: 0.070±0.020 tpm), loses H3K27ac, and acquires H3K27me3 at later stages (GSC: 1.54; 32C NC: 16.7; 512C NC: 13.7) (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: Chinmo encodes a major transcription factor maintaining sexual identity in testis.
claims.source: Chinmo (Figure 3F) encodes a major transcription factor maintaining sexual identity in testis (Flaherty et al., 2010; Grmai et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Flaherty et al., 2010 and Grmai et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Chinmo undergoes E(z)-dependent shutdown and accumulates H3K27me3.
claims.source: It undergoes E(z)-dependent shutdown (DeLuca et al., 2020) and accumulates H3K27me3 (GSC: 0.753; 32C NC: 11.2; 512C NC: 11.3).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data, and a citation to DeLuca et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Always early (aly) is essential for the spermatocyte gene program and has no known female function.
claims.source: Always early (aly) is essential for the spermatocyte gene program, has no known female function, and is likewise repressed in early female germ cells supported by E(z) (H3K27me3 GSC: 0.387; 32C NC: 1.25; 512C NC: 0.901) (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Tdrd5l is implicated in germline male sex regulation.
claims.source: Tdrd5l (Figure 3H), a gene implicated in germline male sex regulation (Primus et al., 2019), is also strongly expressed in female GSCs (82.4±7.02 tpm), and is downregulated before OVS6 (1.72±0.528 tpm) dependent on E(z) and associated with increasing H3K27me3 (GSC: 0.631; 32C NC: 2.87; 512C NC: 2.30).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data, and a citation to Primus et al., 2019.

claims.claim: E(z) downregulates genes preferentially expressed in male accessory gland.
claims.source: In addition to controlling many highly testis-enriched genes, E(z) also downregulates other genes with sexually dimorphic expression, including genes preferentially expressed in male accessory gland.
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Only about 25% of the male-biased genes affected by E(z) are primarily repressed by Polycomb or show increases in gene body H3K27me3 levels as high as those of Polycomb domain targets.
claims.source: However, only about 25% of the male-biased genes affected by E(z) are primarily repressed by Polycomb (i.e. >50%) or show increases in gene body H3K27me3 levels as high as those of Polycomb domain targets, suggesting that the majority of the E(z)-dependent gene repression is indirect.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: ord, corolla, and vilya function in meiosis and are expressed in GSCs and downregulated in young follicles.
claims.source: ord, corolla, and vilya, which function in meiosis, are expressed in GSCs and downregulated in young follicles, although the contribution of E(z) to gene downregulation varies: vilya (38%), ord (20%), and corolla (6.6%).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Phf7 is expressed in GSCs and at higher levels in OVS6 in E(z)[GLKD] compared to control.
claims.source: Phf7 (Figure 3I) is expressed in GSCs (75.1±9.00), and at higher levels in OVS6 in E(z)[GLKD] (62.8±7.15) compared to control (32.4±3.51).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3I.

claims.claim: Phf7 continues to be expressed throughout oogenesis.
claims.source: However, Phf7 continues to be expressed throughout oogenesis (S14nfc: 99.3±5.36).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: High levels of gene expression are often associated with promoter H3K27 acetylation (H3K27ac) catalyzed by CREB-binding protein (CBP).
claims.source: High levels of gene expression are often associated with promoter H3K27 acetylation (H3K27ac) catalyzed by CREB-binding protein (CBP), a conserved histone acetyl transferase (Holmqvist and Mannervik, 2013; reviewed in Lehrmann et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Holmqvist and Mannervik, 2013 and Lehrmann et al., 2002.

claims.claim: Knockdown of nejire in germ cells greatly reduced H3K27ac staining and arrested follicle growth and development beyond stage 1.
claims.source: While GLKD of the white gene in control ovaries had no effect, knockdown of nej in germ cells greatly reduced H3K27ac staining, and arrested follicle growth and development beyond stage 1 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is based on the nejire knockdown experiment shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The conserved germline gene piwi is expressed throughout oogenesis.
claims.source: Chromatin tracks around the conserved germline gene (CGG) piwi which is expressed throughout oogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq and chromatin data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: H3K27me3 does not increase at the piwi locus during oogenesis.
claims.source: H3K27me3 does not increase.
claims.evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Highly expressed genes in GSCs usually have high levels of H3K27ac and low levels of H3K27me3.
claims.source: Highly expressed genes usually had high levels of H3K27ac (and low levels of H3K27me3), while genes expressed at low levels did not.
claims.evidence: This is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: H3K27ac peaks in GSCs were almost always (91%) associated with TSSs.
claims.source: H3K27ac peaks in GSCs were almost always (91%) associated with TSSs (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Most genes with H3K27ac peaks also had ATAC peaks near the TSS that accounted for 68% of total ATAC peaks.
claims.source: Most of these genes also had ATAC peaks near the TSS that accounted for 68% of total ATAC peaks; the remaining ATAC peaks were located in other gene regions, and indicate the location of candidate enhancers.
claims.evidence: This is based on ATAC-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: 101 genes with the highest H3K27ac levels in GSCs cluster in autosomal pericentric regions and in two euchromatic regions.
claims.source: To investigate the GSC transcription program, we identified 101 genes with the highest H3K27ac levels in GSCs (Supplementary file 1c). These genes cluster in autosomal pericentric regions, as well as in two euchromatic regions, 31B-F on chromosome 2L, and in region 13F-14C on the X chromosome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Genes with highest H3K27ac in GSCs encode multiple regulators of germ cell development, the cell cycle, translation, protein stability, and signaling.
claims.source: They encode multiple regulators of germ cell development, the cell cycle (including cdk1 and CycD), translation, protein stability, and signaling.
claims.evidence: This is based on gene annotation analysis of the highly acetylated genes.

claims.claim: H3K27ac is elevated in NC nuclei from young follicles.
claims.source: H3K27ac is elevated in NC nuclei from young follicles (Figure 4F) and at the promoters of many upregulated genes (Figure 4G, pink).
claims.evidence: This is based on immunofluorescence and ChIP-seq data shown in Figures 4F and 4G.

claims.claim: More than 600 genes are increased at least threefold downstream from GSCs in young follicles.
claims.source: Downstream from GSCs in young follicles, we identified more than 600 genes that are increased at least threefold (Supplementary file 1d).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis.

claims.claim: Myc is among the transcription factors that increase sharply in growing follicles.
claims.source: Consistent with previous work (Wang et al., 2019), Myc is among the transcription factors found to increase sharply in growing follicles (OVS6/GSC: 5.1-fold; Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A and cited previous work.

claims.claim: FoxO increases 7.6-fold in young follicles compared to GSCs.
claims.source: FoxO, the mediator of insulin signaling, is also much higher than in GSCs (7.6-fold).
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation is substantially increased beginning in region 2b.
claims.source: Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation is substantially increased beginning in region 2b (Wang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2019.

claims.claim: ATP synthase function during oogenesis is largely independent of ATP production.
claims.source: Previous genetic studies also found that ATP synthase function during oogenesis is largely independent of ATP production (Teixeira et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Teixeira et al., 2015.

claims.claim: A dramatic metabolic shift occurs between GSCs and OVS6 NCs.
claims.source: The GO categories reveal that a dramatic metabolic shift occurs between GSCs and OVS6 NCs.
claims.evidence: This is based on GO analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Glycolytic genes show mostly upregulation but a shutoff of Ldh in young NCs.
claims.source: Expression values (tpm) in GSCs and OVS6 NCs of glycolytic genes showing mostly upregulation but a shutoff of Ldh.
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: More than 40 transmembrane transporters are upregulated at least 10-fold in young NCs.
claims.source: A closer examination of 20 of the more than 40 transmembrane transporters that were upregulated at least 10-fold (Supplementary file 1d) is shown in Figure 5D.
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Sfxn1-3 is upregulated 15-fold in young NCs and its mouse ortholog Sfxn1 encodes the mitochondrial serine transporter.
claims.source: For example, Sfxn1-3 (upregulated 15-fold), whose mouse ortholog is Sfxn1, encodes the mitochondrial serine transporter located in the mitochondrial inner membrane.
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data and knowledge of the mouse ortholog function.

claims.claim: Serine import by Sfxn1 supplies the sole substrate for one-carbon metabolism.
claims.source: Serine import by Sfxn1 supplies the sole substrate for one-carbon metabolism, which generates S-adenosyl methionine (using Sam-S, upregulated 28-fold), glutathione, and NADPH that are needed for methylation, nucleotide biosynthesis, gluconeogenesis, and many other processes (Kory et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kory et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The Dic1/Slc25a10 transporter is increased 23-fold and catalyzes exchanges of dicarboxylates for inorganic phosphate and sulfur-containing compounds in support of gluconeogenesis.
claims.source: The Dic1/Slc25a10 transporter (23-fold increased) encodes another inner membrane protein. It catalyzes exchanges of dicarboxylates for inorganic phosphate and sulfur-containing compounds in support of gluconeogenesis.
claims.evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data and knowledge of transporter function.

claims.claim: Polycomb contributes to repressing a class of genes expressed in GSC daughters for no apparent reason.
claims.source: (1) Polycomb contributes to repressing a class of genes expressed in GSC daughters for no apparent reason.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement based on the E(z) knockdown data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Genes encoding many proteins needed and expressed by stem cells are clustered in centric heterochromatic domains and highly modified with H3K27ac in GSCs.
claims.source: (2) Genes encoding many proteins needed and expressed by stem cells are clustered in centric heterochromatic domains and highly modified with H3K27ac in GSCs.
claims.evidence: This is based on ChIP-seq data showing H3K27ac enrichment in centric regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: A novel mechanism of transposon control used by stem cells is implicated by the initial focus of their daughter cells on syncytial interconnection and H3K9me3-mediated repression.
claims.source: (3) A novel mechanism of transposon control used by stem cells is implicated by the initial focus of their daughter cells on syncytial interconnection and H3K9me3-mediated repression.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the observations about cyst formation and heterochromatin increase.

claims.claim: Animal life cycles require two connected totipotent differentiation processes, rather than just one.
claims.source: (4) Animal life cycles require two connected totipotent differentiation processes, rather than just one.
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual claim based on the comparison of maternal and zygotic developmental trajectories.

claims.claim: The Polycomb-associated downregulation of genes in early Drosophila female germ cells may be analogous to Polycomb regulation during mammalian PGC development.
claims.source: The Polycomb-associated downregulation of genes in early Drosophila female germ cells may be analogous to Polycomb regulation during mammalian PGC development (review: Loh and Veenstra, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative comparison supported by a review citation.

claims.claim: During migration, mouse PGCs significantly reduce their DNA methylation and repressive H3K9me2, but upregulate H3K27me3.
claims.source: During migration, the PGCs significantly reduce their DNA methylation and repressive H3K9me2, but upregulate H3K27me3 (Seki et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seki et al., 2005.

claims.claim: The timing of sex-specific PGC differentiation depends on the PRC2 component EED.
claims.source: The timing of sex-specific PGC differentiation depends on the PRC2 component EED, which may interact with Dnmt1 to regulate this process (Lowe et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lowe et al., 2022.

claims.claim: Mouse PGCs arrest in G2 and modify RNA polymerase tail phosphorylation to repress transcription during part of their migration.
claims.source: During part of this period they arrest in G2 and modify RNA polymerase tail phosphorylation to repress transcription (Seki et al., 2007), changes that also take place in migrating Drosophila PGCs (Su et al., 1998; Deshpande et al., 2004; Martinho et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: These events allow mouse PGCs to reacquire totipotency, reactivate conserved germ cell genes such as Ddx4, and to silence gene expression resulting from somatic signals received prior to their reprogramming as germ cells.
claims.source: These events allow mouse PGCs to reacquire totipotency, reactivate conserved germ cell genes such as Ddx4, and to silence gene expression resulting from somatic signals received prior to their reprogramming as germ cells (Hill et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hill et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Polycomb-dependent silencing in Drosophila may likewise 'clean up' extraneous transcription to compensate for stochastic or incomplete programming at earlier stages.
claims.source: Polycomb-dependent silencing in Drosophila may likewise 'clean up' extraneous transcription to compensate for stochastic or incomplete programming at earlier stages.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the comparison with mouse PGC development.

claims.claim: GSCs and early female germ cells normally express many male germ cell genes.
claims.source: Our finding that GSCs and early female germ cells normally express many male germ cell genes calls into question elevated male gene expression as a criterion for identifying germline sex determination genes (Bhaskar et al., 2022; Grmai et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is based on the RNA-seq data showing expression of testis genes in GSCs.

claims.claim: Mutants that increase testis-related gene expression and also arrest female germ cell development or generate GSC-like tumors may not determine germline sex, because elevated male gene expression is normal in female germ cells at early stages.
claims.source: Mutants that increase testis-related gene expression and also arrest female germ cell development or generate GSC-like tumors may not determine germline sex, because elevated male gene expression is normal in female germ cells at early stages.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that testis genes are normally expressed in early female germ cells.

claims.claim: Overexpression of Phf7 in female germ cells disrupts their differentiation and induces expression of several hundred testis genes.
claims.source: For example, overexpression of the proposed germline sex determination regulator Phf7 (Yang et al., 2012) in female germ cells disrupts their differentiation and induces expression of several hundred testis genes (Shapiro-Kulnane et al., 2015; Smolko et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang et al., 2012, Shapiro-Kulnane et al., 2015, and Smolko et al., 2020.

claims.claim: Testis genes induced by Phf7 overexpression extensively overlap the testis genes normally downregulated by E(z).
claims.source: We find that these genes extensively overlap the testis genes normally downregulated by E(z).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparing gene lists from different studies.

claims.claim: Mutations of stonewall (stwl) disrupt differentiation, alter germline gene expression, and overproduce Phf7.
claims.source: Mutations of stonewall (stwl), encoding a heterochromatin-interacting factor required to maintain GSCs (Clark and McKearin, 1996), also disrupt differentiation, alter germline gene expression, and overproduce Phf7 (Zinshteyn and Barbash, 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Clark and McKearin, 1996 and Zinshteyn and Barbash, 2022.

claims.claim: The testis genes upregulated by stwl mutation strongly overlap those found in normal female GSCs.
claims.source: The testis genes upregulated by stwl mutation strongly overlap those found in normal female GSCs, which itself 'overproduces' Phf7 transcripts.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on comparing gene expression data.

claims.claim: The SKI complex is required for follicle development beyond early follicle stages and degrades some early female germ cell RNAs.
claims.source: The SKI complex is required for follicle development beyond early follicle stages and degrades some early female germ cell RNAs (Blatt et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Blatt et al., 2021.

claims.claim: About 10% of SKI-complex target genes overlap with the E(z)-repressed genes.
claims.source: We find that about 10% of SKI-complex target genes overlap with the E(z)-repressed genes, including RpL22-like and dany.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparing gene lists from different studies.

claims.claim: ovaries absent (ova) is needed for heterochromatin formation and transposon repression in GSC daughters.
claims.source: ovaries absent (ova) is needed for heterochromatin formation and transposon repression in GSC daughters (Yang et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2019.

claims.claim: vasa controls mRNA translation in female germ cells and represses TEs in nuage.
claims.source: vasa controls mRNA translation in female germ cells and represses TEs in nuage.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge of vasa function.

claims.claim: me31B is required to form germ cell P granules.
claims.source: me31B is required to form germ cell P granules (Nakamura et al., 2001), while insulin pathway genes chico, Pten, and Reptor-BP couple GSC activity to nutrients.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nakamura et al., 2001.

claims.claim: daughterless is maternally required for sex determination.
claims.source: daughterless is maternally required for sex determination (Cronmiller and Cline, 1987).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cronmiller and Cline, 1987.

claims.claim: Region 31 forms the unusual 'gooseneck' region of polytene chromosomes and binds high level of HP1a.
claims.source: This region forms the unusual 'gooseneck' region of polytene chromosomes and binds high level of HP1a (James et al., 1989; DeWit et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to James et al., 1989 and DeWit et al., 2007.

claims.claim: Many conserved genes in region 31 are located in heterochromatin in Drosophila virilis and Drosophila pseudoobscura.
claims.source: Many conserved genes in this domain are located in heterochromatin in Drosophila virilis and Drosophila pseudoobscura (Caizzi et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Caizzi et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The syncytial environment in the germline cyst can help control TE activity by allowing piRNAs induced by TE activity in one cyst cell to be shared with other cyst cells.
claims.source: However, the syncytial environment in the germline cyst, whose cells express high levels of piwi/piRNA pathway components (Figure 6B), can also help control TE activity. The presence of a cyst or syncytium would allow piRNAs induced by TE activity in one cyst cell to be shared with the other cyst cells (Figure 6A), enhancing resistance to that TE in the other cells before transposition can occur there (reviews: Huang et al., 2017; Czech et al., 2018; Wang and Lin, 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the syncytial nature of cysts and piRNA biology, supported by review citations.

claims.claim: The high similarity of sister cells recently derived from a common precursor likely enhances the efficacy of piRNA sharing.
claims.source: The high similarity of sister cells recently derived from a common precursor likely enhances the efficacy of such sharing.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference.

claims.claim: Activation of the nuclear arm of the piRNA pathway contributes to the H3K9me3-modified chromatin that increases in GSC daughters as they prepare and enter meiosis.
claims.source: Activation of the nuclear arm of the piRNA pathway contributes to the H3K9me3-modified chromatin that increases in GSC daughters as they prepare and enter meiosis.
claims.evidence: This is based on the ChIP-seq data and knowledge of piRNA pathway function.

claims.claim: H3K9me3 increases utilize piwi and eggless and target transposon-related as well as uniquely mapping sequences.
claims.source: These increases utilize piwi and eggless and target transposon-related as well as uniquely mapping sequences (Figure 2F and G; Clough et al., 2007; Clough et al., 2014; Ninova et al., 2020; Chen and Aravin, 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the data in Figure 2F-G and multiple citations.

claims.claim: Very similar heterochromatin formation takes place during the last few syncytial cleavages of the Drosophila embryo downstream from the zygote.
claims.source: Very similar heterochromatin formation takes place during the last few syncytial cleavages of the Drosophila embryo downstream from the zygote (Lu et al., 1998; Gu and Elgin, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Lu et al., 1998 and Gu and Elgin, 2013.

claims.claim: Heterochromatin formation during early embryogenesis in Drosophila miranda involves piRNA-directed H3K9me3 deposition that may start even earlier in the cleaving pre-blastoderm embryo.
claims.source: Heterochromatin formation during early embryogenesis in Drosophila miranda also involves piRNA-directed H3K9me3 deposition that may start even earlier in the cleaving pre-blastoderm embryo (Wei et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wei et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Drosophila miranda embryos remain syncytial and likely share piRNAs between preblastoderm nuclei, prior to cellularization.
claims.source: These embryos remain syncytial and likely share piRNAs between preblastoderm nuclei, prior to cellularization.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the syncytial nature of early embryos.

claims.claim: The formation of interconnected germline cysts or syncytia just downstream from highly potent stem cells has been extensively conserved in male and female germ cells throughout animal phylogeny.
claims.source: The formation of interconnected germline cysts or syncytia just downstream from highly potent stem cells has been extensively conserved in male and female germ cells throughout animal phylogeny (review: Spradling, 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a review citation.

claims.claim: Cyst formation can be traced back to the highly potent stem cells found in basal animals including hydra, planaria, parasitic flatworms, and other organisms.
claims.source: These events can be traced back to the highly potent stem cells (i.e. interstitial stem cells [ISCs], neoblasts) found in basal animals including hydra, planaria, parasitic flatworms, and other organisms (Zeng et al., 2018; Issigonis and Newmark, 2019; Reddien, 2022; Littlefield, 1994).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: Stem cells in basal eukaryotes express largely the same set of CGGs present in bilaterian animal germ cells.
claims.source: Stem cells in basal eukaryotes express largely the same set of CGGs present in bilaterian animal germ cells (Fierro-Constaín et al., 2017), and frequently also form cysts downstream from highly potent germline and somatic stem cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fierro-Constaín et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Cysts similar to those produced by Drosophila GSC daughters arise downstream from hydra GSCs and immediately downstream from somatic ISC daughters which generate cnidocytes.
claims.source: Notably, cysts similar to those produced by Drosophila GSC daughters not only arise downstream from hydra GSCs (Littlefield, 1994), but immediately downstream from somatic ISC daughters which generate the cnidocytes required for feeding (David, 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Littlefield, 1994 and David, 2012.

claims.claim: The intercellular bridges in cnidoblast cysts resemble germline IBs and were observed to share cytoplasm between cyst members.
claims.source: The intercellular bridges (IBs) in cnidoblast cysts resemble germline IBs and were observed to share cytoplasm between cyst members (Fawcett et al., 1959).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fawcett et al., 1959.

claims.claim: Hydra ISCs, GSCs, and some downstream cells express piwi genes carrying piRNAs that mostly target transposons.
claims.source: Hydra in ISCs, GSCs, and some downstream cells express piwi genes carrying piRNAs that mostly target transposons (Lim et al., 2014), suggesting that cnidoblast cysts also help control TE activity within and downstream from highly potent somatic and germline stem cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lim et al., 2014.

claims.claim: The timing of cyst and heterochromatin formation just after the stem cell state is surprising.
claims.source: The timing of cyst and heterochromatin formation just after the stem cell state is surprising.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretive statement based on the observations.

claims.claim: Potent stem cells and GSCs are collectively immortal and responsible for protecting a species' genome from TEs over developmental time, spanning potentially millions of generations.
claims.source: Potent stem cells and GSCs are collectively immortal and responsible for protecting a species' genome from TEs over developmental time, spanning potentially millions of generations.
claims.evidence: This is based on general knowledge of stem cell biology and evolutionary timescales.

claims.claim: Female Drosophila GSCs display relatively open chromatin and only form a syncytial environment and upregulate heterochromatin in downstream cells.
claims.source: Yet female Drosophila GSCs display relatively open chromatin (DeLuca et al., 2020) and like the Drosophila zygote only form a syncytial environment and upregulate heterochromatin in downstream cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on the data presented in the manuscript and cited previous work.

claims.claim: The timing of heterochromatin formation argues that stem cells use additional mechanisms in addition to the cytoplasmic piwi pathway for transposon control.
claims.source: The timing of these events argues that stem cells use additional mechanisms in addition to the cytoplasmic piwi pathway, for transposon control, that render H3K9me3-mediated heterochromatin formation unnecessary.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the timing of heterochromatin formation.

claims.claim: Stem cell repression mechanisms must fade quickly in daughter cells, necessitating them to increase alternative transposon defense mechanisms.
claims.source: However, this stem cell repression mechanism must fade quickly in daughter cells, necessitating them to increase alternative transposon defense mechanisms.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observed changes in chromatin and gene expression.

claims.claim: In a genetic screen, about 6800 males had zero transposon-containing progeny, 6173 had one offspring with a jump, 1024 had two such progeny, 17 had three, and 2 had four.
claims.source: 100–200 progeny were analyzed from each of ~15,000 individual males. About 6800 had zero transposon-containing progeny, 6173 had one offspring with a jump, 1024 had two such progeny, 17 had three, and 2 had four.
claims.evidence: This is based on data from a genetic screen cited (Karpen and Spradling, 1992).

claims.claim: Overall about 7909 transpositions occurred singly and 367 occurred as doublets in the genetic screen.
claims.source: Progeny with transpositions were then analyzed by enhancer trapping and limited insertion sequencing, indicating that overall about 7909 transpositions occurred singly and that 367 occurred as doublets.
claims.evidence: This is based on data from a genetic screen.

claims.claim: From the 19 males with three or four transposed offspring, only two contained a single sibling with one identical transposition; thus no clusters larger than two were observed.
claims.source: From the 19 males with three or four transposed offspring, only two contained a single sibling with one identical transposition; thus no clusters larger than two were observed.
claims.evidence: This is based on data from a genetic screen.

claims.claim: If P elements had jumped during preadult germ cell development or at the stem cell stage, then each mutant stem cell would have generated clusters amounting to 5–10% of progeny.
claims.source: If P elements had jumped during preadult germ cell development or at the stem cell stage, then each mutant stem cell (from 10 to 20 total) would have generated clusters amounting to 5–10% of progeny, that is 5–20 offspring with identical insertions.
claims.evidence: This is a theoretical calculation based on stem cell biology.

claims.claim: Highly potent stem cells and their immediate progeny frequently have very short G1 and long G2 phases.
claims.source: Such stem cells and their immediate progeny in gonads, embryos, and cell lines frequently have very short G1 and long G2 phases (Hsu et al., 2008; Sheng and Matunis, 2011; Pauklin and Vallier, 2013; Ter Huurne and Stunnenberg, 2021; Ables and Drummond-Barbosa, 2013; Seller et al., 2019; Vogg et al., 2021).

claims.claim: DNA replication during S phase is altered in highly potent stem cells due to changes in the number and order of origin activation.

claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: P elements insert preferentially near replication origins.
claims.source: P elements, for example, insert preferentially near replication origins (Spradling et al., 2011; Cao et al., 2023) and this may allow them to transpose after duplication to a new unfired origin, often in a late replicating region (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Spradling et al., 2011 and Cao et al., 2023.

claims.source: Thus, highly potent stem cells may alter cell cycle and replication properties to enhance their ability to suppress TE movement.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the observations about cell cycle and replication.

claims.source: Early in Drosophila cleavage there is no late S phase, but after cycle 9, derepression of Rap1-binding factor (Rip1) allows Rip1 to bind to and repress satellite DNA duplication, prolonging S phase (Seller and O'Farrell, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seller and O'Farrell, 2018.

claims.claim: DNA replication is temporally regulated to facilitate chromatin epigenetic regulation.
claims.source: The reason DNA replication is temporally regulated is not understood although it is proposed to facilitate chromatin epigenetic regulation (see Klein et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative proposal supported by a citation.

claims.source: Our studies emphasize that two such stem cell differentiation units are required for each generational cycle, rather than one as often visualized (Figure 2H).
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual claim based on the analysis presented in the manuscript.

claims.source: Maternal and zygotic stem cell development act over parts of two animal generations (zygote to zygote) to complete a single generational cycle (GSC to GSC).
claims.evidence: This is a conceptual claim based on the analysis presented in the manuscript.

results.result: Heterochromatin formation, marked by H3K9me3 enrichment, increases in germ cells downstream from GSCs. GSCs show minimal H3K9me3 enrichment in centric regions, but levels increase in region 2a/2b germ cells and further in 4C and 8C nurse cells. H3K9me3 also increases on transposable element sequences during this developmental progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C18 are well-supported by multiple lines of evidence including immunofluorescence (Figure 2A-B) and ChIP-seq data (Figure 2C-D) showing progressive increases in H3K9me3 in centric regions and on TEs as germ cells differentiate from GSCs. The data are internally consistent and supported by prior work (Rangan et al., 2011).

results.result: Heterochromatic reporter genes become repressed during germ cell differentiation in an H3K9me3- and Piwi-dependent manner. Euchromatic hsGFP insertions remain expressed throughout development, while heterochromatic insertions are repressed after 16-cell cyst formation. This repression requires eggless/SETDB1 and Piwi, specifically affecting centric reporters after meiotic onset.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 are supported by hsGFP reporter expression data (Figure 2E-G) showing differential repression based on chromosomal location and developmental stage. The genetic requirements for eggless and Piwi are demonstrated experimentally. The data provide functional validation of the H3K9me3 ChIP-seq results.

results.result: GSC differentiation parallels zygotic development in chromatin dynamics. Both maternal (GSC-derived) and zygotic developmental trajectories involve syncytial stages and upregulated heterochromatin formation. Open chromatin in GSCs/zygotes is followed by heterochromatin increase in cysts/embryonic cleavages, then Polycomb-mediated somatic differentiation.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C33 synthesize the current findings with established knowledge and prior work (DeLuca et al., 2020; multiple citations for embryonic development). The parallel is well-documented through chromatin data (Figure 2H) and supported by extensive literature on both developmental systems. This represents a conceptual advance in understanding stem cell biology.

results.result: GSCs contain altered Polycomb complex composition with high Pcl and low Scm/canonical PRC1/PRC2 subunits, resulting in stochastic H3K27me3 site selection. After follicle formation, Pcl decreases, Scm increases, and canonical Polycomb domains become efficiently repressed in nurse cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 are supported by prior work (DeLuca et al., 2020) that characterized Polycomb complex composition and H3K27me3 patterns. While the current manuscript relies on this citation rather than presenting new data, the claims accurately represent established findings that provide context for the E(z) knockdown experiments.

results.result: E(z) regulates 423 genes that are downregulated during early germ cell differentiation. 78% of these genes show >10-fold downregulation in OVS6 compared to GSCs, with most becoming silent by OVS6 (88%) or mature oocyte (98%). E(z)-regulated genes comprise 40-50% of all genes shut off between GSC and early follicular stages.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C41 are supported by RNA-seq data comparing wild-type and E(z) knockdown samples (Supplementary file 1b). The quantitative thresholds are clearly defined and the percentages are calculated from the data. This establishes the scope of E(z)-dependent gene regulation during differentiation.

results.result: The GSC differentiation gene bgcn shows E(z)-dependent chromatin changes during development. Bgcn has high H3K27ac and ATAC peaks in GSCs/early NCs, but loses H3K27ac and gains H3K27me3 in 32C NCs. Despite 10-fold upregulation in E(z) knockdown, bgcn expression remains only 15% of GSC levels, suggesting additional regulatory mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by integrated chromatin (ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq) and expression data (RNA-seq) shown in Figure 3B. The incomplete rescue by E(z) knockdown (C45) is appropriately interpreted as evidence for additional regulatory pathways. This provides a detailed example of E(z)-mediated gene regulation.

results.result: E(z) downregulates testis-enriched and male-biased genes in female GSCs. 49% of E(z)-regulated genes are predominantly expressed in testis or male accessory gland. Examples include CG43088, escargot, chinmo, aly, and tdrd5l, which show E(z)-dependent repression and H3K27me3 accumulation. However, only ~25% show direct Polycomb repression, suggesting indirect mechanisms predominate.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C56 are supported by tissue expression analysis (Fly Atlas), RNA-seq, and ChIP-seq data (Figure 3C-H). The distinction between direct and indirect E(z) effects (C56) is appropriately made based on H3K27me3 levels. This reveals an unexpected role for Polycomb in sex-specific gene regulation.

results.result: Some testis genes expressed in GSCs have female germ cell functions. Meiotic genes (ord, corolla, vilya) show variable E(z) dependence (6.6-38%). Phf7 is expressed in GSCs, partially E(z)-regulated in OVS6, but continues expression throughout oogenesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 3I for Phf7). These examples demonstrate that not all testis-enriched genes in GSCs are inappropriately expressed, and that E(z) regulation varies by gene. This nuances the interpretation of male gene expression in female germ cells.

results.result: Nejire/CBP is essential for H3K27 acetylation and follicle development. Knockdown of nejire in germ cells greatly reduces H3K27ac staining and arrests follicle development beyond stage 1, while white gene knockdown has no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C61 are supported by the nejire knockdown experiment (Figure 4A) showing loss of H3K27ac and developmental arrest. The white gene serves as an appropriate negative control. This establishes the functional importance of H3K27ac for germ cell development.

results.result: H3K27ac marks highly expressed genes in GSCs. The conserved germline gene piwi maintains expression without H3K27me3 increase. Genome-wide, highly expressed genes have high H3K27ac and low H3K27me3. 91% of H3K27ac peaks associate with TSSs, and 68% of ATAC peaks co-localize with H3K27ac peaks at TSSs.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C66 are supported by ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data (Figure 4B-D). The correlation between H3K27ac and gene expression (C64) is shown in Figure 4C. The peak distribution analysis (C65-C66) provides genome-wide validation. This establishes H3K27ac as a marker of active transcription in GSCs.

results.result: The 101 genes with highest H3K27ac in GSCs cluster in autosomal pericentric regions and two euchromatic regions (31B-F on 2L, 13F-14C on X). These genes encode regulators of germ cell development, cell cycle (cdk1, CycD), translation, protein stability, and signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by ChIP-seq data analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1c). The chromosomal clustering is clearly demonstrated and the functional categories are based on gene annotation. This reveals spatial organization of highly active genes in GSCs.

results.result: H3K27ac increases in young nurse cell nuclei and at promoters of upregulated genes. More than 600 genes increase at least threefold downstream from GSCs in young follicles.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C70 are supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 4F), ChIP-seq (Figure 4G), and RNA-seq data (Supplementary file 1d). The correlation between H3K27ac changes and gene expression changes validates the functional significance of this modification during differentiation.

results.result: Transcription factors and metabolic regulators increase in growing follicles. Myc increases 5.1-fold and FoxO increases 7.6-fold in OVS6 compared to GSCs. Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation increases beginning in region 2b, though ATP synthase function is largely independent of ATP production.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 5A). Claims C73-C74 are supported by citations to prior work (Wang et al., 2019; Teixeira et al., 2015). The integration of current and prior findings provides context for metabolic reprogramming.

results.result: A dramatic metabolic shift occurs between GSCs and young nurse cells. GO analysis reveals upregulation of transmembrane transport, amino acid metabolism, gluconeogenesis, and lipid metabolism. Glycolytic genes are mostly upregulated except Ldh which is shut down. More than 40 transmembrane transporters increase ≥10-fold, including Sfxn1-3 (15-fold, mitochondrial serine transporter) and Dic1 (23-fold, dicarboxylate transporter supporting gluconeogenesis).
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 are supported by GO analysis (Figure 5B) and RNA-seq data (Figure 5C-D, Supplementary file 1d). The specific examples (Sfxn1-3, Dic1) are well-documented with fold-changes and functional annotations. The metabolic shift is comprehensively characterized at the transcriptional level.

results.result: Four major insights emerge from this study: (1) Polycomb represses genes in GSC daughters for unclear reasons; (2) Stem cell genes cluster in centric heterochromatic domains with high H3K27ac; (3) Syncytial cyst formation and H3K9me3 repression represent a novel transposon control mechanism; (4) Animal life cycles require two connected totipotent differentiation processes.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C84 accurately summarize the major findings supported by data throughout the manuscript. C81 is supported by E(z) knockdown data, C82 by H3K27ac ChIP-seq, C83 by heterochromatin and cyst formation data, and C84 by the comparative analysis of maternal and zygotic development. These represent the key conceptual advances.

results.result: Polycomb-mediated gene repression in Drosophila female germ cells may parallel mammalian PGC development. Mouse PGCs reduce DNA methylation and H3K9me2 but upregulate H3K27me3 during migration, arrest in G2, and repress transcription. These events enable totipotency reacquisition and silencing of somatic gene expression. Drosophila Polycomb silencing may similarly 'clean up' extraneous transcription.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C90 draw parallels between Drosophila and mammalian systems based on citations (C86-C89) and speculation (C85, C90). While the comparison is plausible and supported by literature, direct experimental evidence linking the mechanisms is lacking. The analogy is reasonable but remains speculative without cross-species validation.

results.result: GSCs normally express many male germ cell genes, challenging the use of elevated male gene expression as a criterion for identifying sex determination genes. Mutants that increase testis gene expression and arrest development (e.g., Phf7 overexpression, stonewall mutations) may not determine germline sex since male gene expression is normal in early female germ cells. Testis genes induced by these perturbations overlap with genes normally downregulated by E(z).
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C96 are supported by RNA-seq data showing testis gene expression in GSCs (C91) and by comparisons with published gene lists from Phf7 and stonewall studies (C93-C96). The inference that these genes may not be sex determination factors (C92) is logical given the data, though it challenges prior interpretations. This represents an important reinterpretation of existing genetic data.

results.result: About 10% of SKI complex target genes overlap with E(z)-repressed genes, including RpL22-like and dany. The SKI complex is required for follicle development beyond early stages and degrades some early female germ cell RNAs.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 are supported by a citation (Blatt et al., 2021) and comparison of gene lists. The modest overlap (10%) is appropriately noted. This provides context for understanding multiple pathways regulating gene expression during germ cell development.

results.result: Genes with high H3K27ac in GSCs include factors with established functions: ova (heterochromatin formation/TE repression), vasa (translation/TE repression), me31B (P granule formation), insulin pathway genes (nutrient sensing), and daughterless (sex determination). Region 31 forms the 'gooseneck' polytene region, binds HP1a, and contains genes located in heterochromatin in other Drosophila species.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C104 are supported by citations for gene functions and chromosomal features. These claims provide biological context for the highly acetylated genes identified in the study, connecting chromatin state to known gene functions and evolutionary conservation.

results.result: Syncytial germline cysts may control TE activity by sharing piRNAs between connected cells. Cyst cells express high levels of piwi/piRNA pathway components, and piRNAs induced by TE activity in one cell could be shared with other cyst cells before transposition occurs. The nuclear piRNA pathway contributes to H3K9me3 increases in GSC daughters, utilizing piwi and eggless to target TEs and unique sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C108 combine speculation (C105-C106) with data (C107-C108). The piRNA sharing hypothesis is plausible given syncytial structure and supported by review citations. The role of nuclear piRNA pathway (C107-C108) is supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 2F-G) and multiple citations. The model is well-reasoned though the piRNA sharing mechanism lacks direct experimental validation.

results.result: Similar heterochromatin formation occurs during late syncytial cleavages in Drosophila embryos. In D. miranda, piRNA-directed H3K9me3 deposition may begin in pre-blastoderm embryos, which remain syncytial and likely share piRNAs between nuclei before cellularization.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C111 are supported by citations to prior work on embryonic heterochromatin formation. The inference about piRNA sharing in syncytial embryos (C111) is reasonable given the established syncytial nature of early embryos. This extends the parallel between maternal and zygotic development.

results.result: Germline cyst formation downstream from highly potent stem cells is conserved throughout animal phylogeny, including basal animals (hydra, planaria). Stem cells in basal organisms express conserved germline genes and form cysts downstream from both germline and somatic stem cells. Hydra cysts resemble Drosophila cysts, with intercellular bridges that share cytoplasm, and express piwi genes with piRNAs targeting transposons.
results.evaluation: Claims C112-C117 are supported by multiple citations documenting cyst formation and piRNA expression across phylogeny. This establishes the evolutionary conservation of the cyst-based TE control mechanism and supports its fundamental importance in stem cell biology.

results.result: The timing of heterochromatin formation just after the stem cell state is surprising given that GSCs are collectively immortal and responsible for protecting genomes from TEs over evolutionary time. GSCs display relatively open chromatin and only upregulate heterochromatin in downstream cells, suggesting stem cells use additional TE control mechanisms that render H3K9me3-mediated heterochromatin unnecessary. These mechanisms must fade quickly in daughter cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C122 present a logical argument based on the chromatin data (C120, supported by current and prior work) and evolutionary considerations (C119, general knowledge). The inference that additional TE control mechanisms exist in GSCs (C121-C122) is reasonable given the data, though the specific mechanisms remain speculative. This represents an important conceptual insight.

results.result: Cluster analysis of P element transposition in a genetic screen shows that transposition is rare at the stem cell stage but begins before cyst formation ends. Of ~15,000 males analyzed, most had 0-1 transposed offspring, with 7909 single transpositions and 367 doublets. No clusters larger than two were observed. If transposition occurred at the GSC stage, 5-20 offspring per male would show identical insertions, which was not observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C123-C127 are supported by data from a genetic screen (Karpen and Spradling, 1992). The cluster size analysis and theoretical calculations (C126) are appropriate. The inference that P elements transpose less frequently at the GSC stage (C127) is well-supported by the absence of large clusters. This provides functional evidence for enhanced TE control in stem cells.

results.result: Transposon activity increases downstream from the zygote. TE transcription is high in early Drosophila, mouse, and human embryos, with particular retroelement classes showing temporal and tissue-specific expression patterns. TE expression patterns can indicate developmental state in stem cell lines, and TE-dependent transcription may be functionally important in early embryonic cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C132 are supported by multiple citations documenting TE expression in early embryos across species. This provides comparative evidence that TE control is relaxed downstream from totipotent states, supporting the model that stem cells have enhanced TE resistance.

results.result: Intrinsic TE resistance in high potency states might explain why DNA methylation can be reduced during PGC reprogramming to pluripotency.
results.evaluation: Claim C133 is speculative, though supported by a citation (Hill et al., 2018) documenting DNA methylation reduction. The causal link between TE resistance and methylation reduction is inferred but not directly tested. This represents a plausible hypothesis requiring further validation.

results.result: Highly potent stem cells may alter cell cycle and DNA replication to suppress TE movement. These cells frequently have short G1 and long G2 phases, and altered S phase with changes in origin activation, replication timing, and elongation rate. P elements insert preferentially near replication origins, potentially transposing to late-replicating regions. Eliminating late S phase might disrupt transposition by removing available targets.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C135 are supported by multiple citations documenting cell cycle and replication differences. Claims C136-C138 present a mechanistic model for how replication timing affects P element transposition, supported by citations (C136) but largely speculative (C137-C138). The model is plausible but lacks direct experimental validation in the stem cell context.

results.result: Replication timing changes during development. Early Drosophila cleavage lacks late S phase, but Rip1 derepression after cycle 9 allows satellite DNA repression and S phase prolongation. Mouse ES cells replicate pericentromeric heterochromatin early-to-mid S phase, but late upon differentiation, associated with reduced H3K9/H3K8 acetylation. The reason for temporal replication regulation is unclear, though proposed to facilitate epigenetic regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C140 are supported by citations documenting replication timing changes. Claim C141 acknowledges uncertainty while citing a speculative proposal. These claims provide context for understanding how replication timing might affect TE control, though the functional significance remains incompletely understood.

results.result: Two stem cell differentiation units are required for each generational cycle. Maternal and zygotic stem cell development act over parts of two animal generations to complete a single generational cycle (GSC to GSC). The embryo cannot replace all maternal germline events. Restoring immortality likely represents the major focus of the maternal program, with rejuvenation occupying most of oogenesis and continuing during embryonic development.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C146 present a conceptual framework based on the integrated analysis of maternal and zygotic development (Figure 2H). While speculative regarding the 'focus' of the maternal program (C145), the claims are well-supported by the data showing distinct but connected developmental trajectories. This represents an important conceptual advance.

results.result: Maternal contributions during oogenesis have lasting effects on embryonic development. Metabolic perturbations during oogenesis affect the zygote, maternal Piwi is essential for embryonic germ cell development and fertility, and Polycomb function during oogenesis is needed for normal mouse embryonic development.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C149 are supported by citations documenting maternal effects on embryonic development. These claims provide evidence that the maternal developmental program has consequences extending into the next generation, supporting the importance of the two-cycle model.

results.result: Gene expression diversity is highest in GSCs and decreases during development. Among genes expressed in mature S14 oocytes, 95% of maternal effect genes and 99% of total transcripts are already expressed in GSCs. About 50% of maternal effect genes are within twofold of final values at the GSC stage, and 80% increase less than fourfold.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C154 are supported by RNA-seq data analysis (Figure 1C, 1E). These findings establish that GSCs already express most genes needed for oogenesis, consistent with the importance of translational control. This provides important context for understanding the transcriptional program of GSCs.

results.result: GSCs have relatively open chromatin with low H3K9me3 levels, but H3K9me3-rich heterochromatin increases in differentiating germ cells beginning at the 16-cell cyst stage. This increase occurs on centric regions and transposable elements, and depends on the H3K9 methylase eggless/SETDB1 and Piwi. Reporter assays confirm that heterochromatic regions become repressed after the GSC stage in a piwi- and eggless-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding, stating 'the data strongly support the conclusions (1) that GSCs have more open chromatin than its differentiating daughter cells, (2) that H3K9me3 heterochromatin forms in 16-cell cyst stage and silences GSC-enriched genes, transposons, and testis-biased and somatic genes.' Multiple complementary methods including ChIP-seq, immunofluorescence, and reporter assays are noted as validating the increase of H3K9me3 during meiosis.

results.result: GSC differentiation during oogenesis parallels zygotic differentiation during early embryogenesis. Both processes occur in syncytial environments (germline cysts or embryonic cleavage divisions) and involve upregulated heterochromatin formation. Open chromatin characteristic of GSCs and zygotes is transient, followed by heterochromatin increases and eventual Polycomb-mediated repression in somatic differentiation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recognize this parallel as a key finding, noting that 'the conclusions are strongly supported by a substantial amount of data' and that the study 'extends a parallel previously noted between stem cell differentiation downstream from the GSC during oogenesis and differentiation downstream from the zygote during early embryogenesis.' The comparison is treated as a significant conceptual contribution.

results.result: Polycomb (E(z)/PRC2) represses a substantial fraction (40-50%) of genes that shut off between GSCs and early follicular stages. Many E(z)-regulated genes are testis-enriched or male-biased genes that are transiently expressed in female GSCs and early germ cells. E(z)-dependent repression is associated with loss of H3K27ac and gain of H3K27me3 at these loci, though only ~25% show direct Polycomb repression, suggesting indirect mechanisms also contribute.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'the data strongly support the conclusions...that H3K9me3 heterochromatin forms in 16-cell cyst stage and silences GSC-enriched genes, transposons, and testis-biased and somatic genes.' The study is noted to 'uncover new biology' regarding gene regulation during GSC differentiation, and the conclusions are described as 'strongly supported by a substantial amount of data.'

results.result: High gene expression in GSCs is associated with promoter H3K27 acetylation (H3K27ac) catalyzed by Neijre/CBP. Knockdown of nejire reduces H3K27ac and arrests follicle development. Genes with the highest H3K27ac levels in GSCs cluster in autosomal pericentric regions and encode regulators of germ cell development, cell cycle, translation, and signaling. H3K27ac peaks are predominantly at transcription start sites.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm that 'the data strongly support the conclusions...(3) that GSC-enriched genes encoding cell cycle control, protein synthesis and signal transduction reside in clusters in autosomal pericentric regions.' The study is noted to uncover 'new biology, notably the proximity of stem cell genes to centric heterochromatin and its regulation,' indicating reviewer acceptance of these chromatin organization findings.

results.result: A dramatic metabolic shift occurs during GSC differentiation, with Neijre/CBP and Myc upregulating growth and reprogramming metabolism. More than 600 genes increase at least threefold in young follicles, including transcription factors (Myc, FoxO) and metabolic genes. Changes include upregulation of glycolytic genes (except Ldh), transmembrane transporters (>40 genes upregulated ≥10-fold), mitochondrial transport, and gluconeogenesis pathways.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'the data strongly support the conclusions...(4) that there is a transcriptionally-driven metabolic reprogramming of nurse (germline) cells to aerobic glycolysis.' This metabolic reprogramming is recognized as one of the major supported findings of the study.

results.result: Gene expression diversity is highest in GSCs and decreases during differentiation. Most maternal effect genes (95%) and total transcripts (99%) expressed in mature oocytes are already expressed in GSCs, with ~50% of maternal effect genes already at near-final RNA levels in GSCs and 80% increasing less than fourfold, consistent with the importance of translational regulation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note that 'GSCs exhibit an open chromatin state and express a large number of genes. However, during differentiation, the number of genes expressed decreases,' indicating acceptance of this finding. The observation is treated as part of the overall characterization of GSC gene expression patterns that reviewers find well-supported.

results.result: The syncytial germline cyst environment enables a novel transposon control mechanism by allowing piRNAs induced by TE activity in one cyst cell to be shared with other cyst cells, enhancing resistance before transposition occurs. This mechanism involves activation of the nuclear piRNA pathway and piwi/eggless-dependent H3K9me3 deposition targeting transposons and unique sequences.
results.evaluation: Reviewers note 'key observations include the low H3K9me3 levels on transposons in GSCs, which warrant further investigation,' indicating interest in and implicit acceptance of the transposon control findings. The mechanistic proposal about syncytial piRNA sharing is treated as a novel contribution, though reviewers suggest it merits further study.

results.result: GSCs and early female germ cells normally express many male germ cell genes, which are subsequently downregulated by E(z). This finding challenges the use of elevated male gene expression as a criterion for identifying germline sex determination genes, as mutants that increase testis gene expression may simply disrupt normal developmental repression rather than determine sex.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recognize this as part of the study's contribution to understanding gene regulation during GSC differentiation. The finding is implicitly supported through the overall positive assessment that 'the conclusions are strongly supported by a substantial amount of data' and the recognition that the study provides 'further insights into critical molecular events during GSC differentiation.'

results.result: The totipotent stem cell state was shaped by the need to resist transposon activity over evolutionary timescales. The timing of heterochromatin formation just after the stem cell stage suggests GSCs use additional transposon control mechanisms beyond H3K9me3-mediated heterochromatin, which must fade quickly in daughter cells. Evidence from P element transposition patterns supports reduced transposition at the stem cell stage.
results.evaluation: While reviewers note 'key observations include the low H3K9me3 levels on transposons in GSCs, which warrant further investigation,' the evolutionary and mechanistic interpretations are largely speculative. Reviewers do not explicitly evaluate these broader theoretical claims, though they accept the underlying observational data about heterochromatin timing and transposon control.

results.result: Animal life cycles require two connected totipotent differentiation processes (maternal and zygotic) rather than one. Maternal and zygotic stem cell development act over parts of two animal generations to complete a single generational cycle. The maternal stem cell program focuses on restoring potential immortality, with rejuvenation occupying most of oogenesis and continuing during embryonic development.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recognize this conceptual framework as a significant contribution, noting that the work 'significantly advances our comprehension of the molecular events occurring during germline stem cell differentiation.' The parallel between maternal and zygotic processes is explicitly acknowledged as well-supported, though the broader theoretical implications are treated as interpretive rather than directly tested.

results.result: Polycomb-associated downregulation in Drosophila female germ cells may be analogous to Polycomb regulation during mammalian PGC development, where PGCs reduce DNA methylation and H3K9me2 but upregulate H3K27me3, and where PRC2 component EED affects sex-specific differentiation timing. This may represent a conserved mechanism to 'clean up' extraneous transcription.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not explicitly evaluate this comparative analysis with mammalian systems. While the Drosophila findings are strongly supported, the analogies to mammalian PGC development are presented as speculative comparisons based on literature citations rather than direct experimental evidence in this study.
